HR-QoL was consistently impaired across studies, most prominently in vitality, energy, and physical functioning domains, with female sex and greater autoimmune comorbidity predicting worse outcomes. Modified-release hydrocortisone and infusion strategies showed more consistent improvements on disease-specific HR-QoL instruments than generic measures, while anxiety and depressive symptoms were generally mild and inconsistently elevated — though mental fatigue and subjective executive dysfunction emerged as more reproducible concerns.
items.caveat: Most included studies were observational and cross-sectional, and many used mixed PAI cohorts where autoimmune etiology was predominant but not exclusive. Heterogeneity in outcome instruments limits direct comparison across studies, and interventional trial data remain sparse.
items.quiz_question: A 34-year-old woman with autoimmune Addison's disease on standard twice-daily hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone reports persistent fatigue and cognitive 'fogginess' despite normal electrolytes and a morning cortisol consistent with adequate replacement. According to this systematic review, what patient-level characteristics are associated with poorer HR-QoL, and what therapeutic modification has shown the most consistent benefit on disease-specific quality-of-life measures?
items.quiz_answer: Female sex and the presence of additional autoimmune comorbidities were repeatedly associated with poorer perceived HR-QoL in this review. Among therapeutic approaches, modified-release hydrocortisone and continuous subcutaneous hydrocortisone infusion strategies demonstrated more consistent improvements on disease-specific HR-QoL instruments compared to standard immediate-release regimens, making these worth considering in patients with persistent impairment despite biochemically adequate replacement.

items.title: Surgical management of ectopic Cushing's syndrome from a pulmonary carcinoid secreting CRH supported by intraoperative ACTH monitoring - a case report.
items.summary: This case report describes a 36-year-old man with ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism in whom dynamic testing (high-dose DST, metyrapone, desmopressin) yielded inconclusive results that could not reliably distinguish Cushing's disease from ectopic Cushing's syndrome (ECS). A small pulmonary nodule was identified on chest imaging, and given the rapid clinical course, surgical resection was pursued with intraoperative ACTH monitoring; a transient ACTH surge during initial excision prompted extension to upper lobectomy, after which ACTH fell markedly and sustained. Pathology confirmed a typical pulmonary carcinoid, and the patient achieved biochemical remission with gradual HPA axis recovery — illustrating intraoperative ACTH monitoring as a potentially valuable adjunct for surgical decision-making in ambiguous ECS.
items.caveat: This is a single case report and cannot support broad practice change. The value of intraoperative ACTH monitoring in ECS remains debated, and the threshold criteria for interpreting intraoperative ACTH changes in this setting are not yet standardized.
items.quiz_question: A 40-year-old woman has biochemical ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism. High-dose dexamethasone suppression, CRH stimulation, and desmopressin tests are all inconclusive. Pituitary MRI is negative; chest CT shows a 9-mm pulmonary nodule. IPSS is equivocal. What does this case suggest about the role of intraoperative ACTH monitoring if thoracic surgery is undertaken, and what intraoperative finding prompted extension of the resection in this report?
items.quiz_answer: This case suggests intraoperative ACTH monitoring can serve as an adjunctive real-time tool for confirming complete resection of a hormone-secreting tumor when preoperative localization is uncertain. In this report, a transient ACTH surge observed during initial tumor excision, without a subsequent sustained decline, indicated incomplete resection and prompted extension to upper lobectomy; a marked and sustained fall in ACTH followed, confirming complete removal.

items.title: Post-dexamethasone cortisol levels in non-functioning adrenal incidentalomas: a pooled individual participant data analysis.
items.summary: This pooled individual participant data analysis of 1,681 subjects (915 NFAI, 766 controls) found that even patients meeting the current NFAI definition (1mg-DST cortisol <1.8 µg/dL) had statistically higher post-DST cortisol and lower ACTH than matched controls, supporting the concept of a continuum of subtle autonomous cortisol secretion below the current diagnostic threshold. Importantly, no alternative F-1mgDST threshold performed with accuracy exceeding 60% for distinguishing NFAI from controls; the best-performing cutoff (1.1 µg/dL) yielded only 55% sensitivity and 57% specificity. The >40% overlap in cortisol values between groups underscores that the 1.8 µg/dL threshold is a population-level convention, not a clean biological boundary. These findings challenge the binary NFAI classification and reinforce the need to integrate clinical context—cardiometabolic and skeletal risk factors—rather than relying on a single cortisol cutoff.
items.caveat: Pooled study design introduces heterogeneity across seven contributing cohorts with varying inclusion criteria (T2D, osteoporosis, hypertension, incidentaloma cohorts mixed as 'controls'). Propensity-score matching was performed but residual confounding cannot be excluded; sample size of each contributing study was not individually reported.
items.quiz_question: A 61-year-old woman with hypertension and a 2.2 cm adrenal incidentaloma has a 1mg-DST cortisol of 1.3 µg/dL, which your lab reports as 'normal suppression.' Based on this pooled analysis, how should you interpret this result and counsel her?
items.quiz_answer: A post-DST cortisol of 1.3 µg/dL falls below the 1.8 µg/dL threshold conventionally defining autonomous cortisol secretion, but this analysis shows that NFAI patients as a group have significantly higher F-1mgDST values than controls even within the 'normal' range, and no threshold below 1.8 µg/dL identifies NFAI with clinically useful accuracy (best AUC ~60%). Clinically, the result should not be used alone to exclude subtle cortisol excess; her cardiometabolic risk profile (hypertension) warrants continued surveillance and integrated risk assessment rather than reassurance based solely on this cortisol value.

items.title: Transition to once-weekly growth hormone in paediatric isolated growth hormone deficiency: a real-world experience.
items.summary: This single-centre retrospective study of 73 children with isolated GHD transitioning from daily rhGH to once-weekly somatrogon demonstrates that height SDS continued to increase and height velocity SDS remained positive at 6, 12, and 18 months post-transition, supporting real-world effectiveness comparable to trial data. A notable finding was a transient but significant rise in BMI SDS during the first year that stabilized by 18 months, and an early IGF-1 SDS peak at 6 months followed by subsequent decline—both warranting monitoring during dose titration. This is among the first real-world cohorts to characterize the metabolic trajectory of somatrogon in a pediatric GHD population outside of a controlled trial.
items.caveat: Single-centre retrospective design with no concurrent control arm; only 27 of 73 patients had reached 18 months of follow-up at data collection, limiting longer-term conclusions. The transient BMI and IGF-1 changes need further characterization in larger cohorts before definitive dose-titration guidance can be derived.
items.quiz_question: You are transitioning a 13-year-old boy with isolated GHD from daily somatropin to once-weekly somatrogon. At his 6-month visit, his IGF-1 SDS is +2.8 and his BMI SDS has risen from +0.5 to +1.1. How do the findings of this real-world study inform your management?
items.quiz_answer: The study found that IGF-1 SDS peaks at 6 months after transition to somatrogon then declines, and BMI SDS rises significantly in the first year before stabilizing by 18 months. An early IGF-1 overshoot is therefore a recognized pattern and may warrant dose adjustment to avoid sustained supraphysiologic IGF-1 exposure. The BMI rise warrants monitoring but is expected to stabilize; dietary and activity counseling is appropriate. Continued close follow-up at 12 and 18 months is supported by this dataset.

items.title: Testosterone and DHEA-S Secreting Adrenal Cortical Adenoma in a Postmenopausal Woman: A Rare Functional Incidentaloma.
items.summary: This case report describes a 53-year-old postmenopausal woman with progressive virilization (hirsutism, alopecia, clitoromegaly), markedly elevated testosterone and DHEA-S, and suppressed gonadotropins, ultimately found to have a 3.5 cm left adrenal cortical adenoma secreting both testosterone and DHEA-S. Preoperative imaging was atypical for adenoma (HU >10, no signal drop on out-of-phase MRI), illustrating that androgen-secreting cortical adenomas can mimic malignancy radiologically; Ki-67 <3% and favorable immunohistochemistry confirmed benignity. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy normalized androgens, and cosyntropin stimulation testing appropriately excluded co-secretory adrenal insufficiency postoperatively.
items.caveat: Single case report; limited generalizability. The atypical imaging phenotype of this adenoma (no intracellular lipid on MRI) reinforces existing literature that adrenal imaging characteristics alone cannot exclude malignancy in androgen-secreting lesions, but no new systematic data are provided.
items.quiz_question: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a 6-month history of hirsutism and clitoromegaly. Labs show testosterone 280 ng/dL, DHEA-S 620 µg/dL, suppressed LH and FSH, normal cortisol suppression on 1mg-DST, and negative pelvic ultrasound. CT shows a 3.2 cm left adrenal mass with 34 HU precontrast. What is the next most appropriate step, and what pathology should be excluded before adrenalectomy?
items.quiz_answer: The clinical and biochemical picture is consistent with an androgen-secreting adrenal tumor; the elevated HU precontrast raises concern for adrenocortical carcinoma, though adenoma remains possible. Before proceeding to adrenalectomy, pheochromocytoma must be biochemically excluded (plasma/urine metanephrines), primary aldosteronism screened if clinically indicated, and significant cortisol co-secretion assessed (already done here). MRI with chemical shift and 18F-FDG PET or adrenal venous sampling may further characterize the lesion. Given the virilization and atypical imaging, surgical resection with histopathological staging (Weiss score, Ki-67, margins) is appropriate.
items.journal: Journal of investigative medicine high impact case reports

items.title: Cortisol Cutoffs for Adrenal Insufficiency Using Elecsys II: A Systematic Review.
items.summary: This systematic review of six studies (1,799 samples, 430 patients) evaluated peak cortisol thresholds for the standard-dose ACTH stimulation test using the Roche Elecsys II monoclonal immunoassay. The authors recommend a revised peak cortisol cutoff of 405 nmol/L (14.7 µg/dL), substantially lower than the historical 500 nmol/L threshold derived from polyclonal assays. The lower threshold reflects reduced cross-reactivity of modern monoclonal assays and is intended to minimize false-negative diagnoses of adrenal insufficiency. This has direct implications for labs and clinicians still applying the legacy cutoff.
items.caveat: Only six studies with a combined 430 patients were available; evidence quality was rated as low by GRADE. The recommended cutoff is specific to the Roche Elecsys II platform and cannot be extrapolated to other assays without independent validation.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old woman with suspected secondary adrenal insufficiency undergoes a standard-dose ACTH stimulation test. Her laboratory uses the Roche Elecsys II immunoassay. Her peak cortisol is 420 nmol/L at 30 minutes. Using the legacy polyclonal threshold of 500 nmol/L she would be labeled insufficient; using the updated monoclonal threshold, how should her result be interpreted, and what does this systematic review recommend?
items.quiz_answer: Using the revised threshold of 405 nmol/L (14.7 µg/dL) recommended for the Elecsys II assay, a peak of 420 nmol/L exceeds the cutoff and would be interpreted as a normal (sufficient) response, arguing against adrenal insufficiency. The review specifically affirms lowering the threshold from 500 nmol/L when using monoclonal assays, to reduce false-negatives while recognizing that 420 nmol/L sits close to the boundary and clinical context remains important.

items.title: Adrenal Masses in a Moroccan Tertiary Center: A 14-Year Retrospective Study of 200 Patients.
items.summary: This 14-year single-center retrospective study from Morocco characterized 200 patients with adrenal masses, finding that incidentaloma was the most common presentation (55%). The etiological breakdown revealed non-secreting adenoma as the most frequent diagnosis (36.5%), followed by pheochromocytoma (16.5%), Conn's adenoma (11%), cortisol-secreting adenoma (10%), and adrenocortical carcinoma (9%). Notably, pheochromocytoma accounted for a markedly higher proportion than typically reported in Western series, and adrenocortical carcinoma represented 9% of the cohort — a proportion worth attention in resource-limited settings where imaging-guided surveillance may be delayed.
items.caveat: Single-center, retrospective design from a tertiary referral center in a developing country context introduces significant selection bias; the case mix likely overrepresents malignant and secretory lesions compared with community-based incidentaloma registries. Surveillance and follow-up data were incomplete for a substantial proportion of patients.
items.quiz_question: In a tertiary endocrinology referral center, what was the second most common diagnosis among 200 patients presenting with adrenal masses in this Moroccan cohort, and what fraction of the overall cohort did adrenocortical carcinoma represent?
items.quiz_answer: Pheochromocytoma was the second most common diagnosis at 16.5%. Adrenocortical carcinoma accounted for 9% (18 of 200 patients) — a higher proportion than typically seen in Western population-based incidentaloma series, likely reflecting referral bias toward symptomatic or radiologically suspicious lesions at a tertiary center.

items.title: Acromegaly as the Initial Presentation of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1: A Case Report.
items.summary: This case report describes a 34-year-old woman whose first clinical manifestation of MEN-1 was a recurrent GH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma presenting as acromegaly, with concurrent hypercalcemia due to a parathyroid adenoma identified on workup. Genetic analysis confirmed a rare pathogenic MEN-1 variant. The case reinforces that while primary hyperparathyroidism is the classic initial MEN-1 feature, acromegaly can occasionally be the presenting syndrome, and the co-occurrence of a pituitary adenoma with hypercalcemia should reliably trigger MEN-1 evaluation regardless of family history.
items.caveat: Single case report; no generalizable frequency data. The rare pathogenic variant identified adds genotype-phenotype interest but cannot support broader prevalence claims. Management followed standard sporadic pituitary adenoma principles with multidisciplinary overlay.
items.quiz_question: A 34-year-old woman presents with enlarging hands, jaw prominence, and elevated IGF-1 confirmed on MRI as a pituitary macroadenoma. Routine labs show serum calcium of 11.4 mg/dL. What syndrome should be actively investigated, and what initial steps would confirm it?
items.quiz_answer: MEN-1 should be suspected given the combination of a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma and hypercalcemia (suggesting primary hyperparathyroidism). Evaluation should include parathyroid hormone level, neck imaging to identify parathyroid adenoma(s), pancreatic imaging/hormonal assessment for islet cell involvement, and germline MEN-1 gene mutation testing — even in the absence of a family history, as demonstrated in this case.
items.journal: The American journal of case reports

items.title: Unilateral adrenal haemorrhage during bridging anticoagulation in primary antiphospholipid syndrome: a case-based review.
items.summary: This case report and literature review describes a 42-year-old man with primary antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) who developed acute unilateral adrenal hemorrhage during peri-procedural bridging anticoagulation with enoxaparin. The patient remained hemodynamically stable and did not develop adrenal insufficiency, and was managed conservatively with careful reintroduction of anticoagulation. The accompanying review highlights that bridging anticoagulation represents a particularly vulnerable window for adrenal hemorrhage in high-risk APS patients, and emphasizes that early CT/MRI and formal adrenal function assessment are essential when APS patients present with abdominal pain during anticoagulation transitions.
items.caveat: Single case report with a narrative review of prior cases; evidence base is limited to case-level data and cannot establish incidence or guide protocol-level recommendations. Adrenal insufficiency did not develop here, so the review may underrepresent cases with more severe adrenal compromise.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with primary antiphospholipid syndrome on long-term warfarin develops acute right upper-quadrant pain during a peri-procedural switch to bridging enoxaparin. What diagnosis should be actively excluded, what imaging is most appropriate, and what adrenal function assessment should be performed?
items.quiz_answer: Adrenal hemorrhage should be actively excluded. CT (or MRI) of the abdomen is the appropriate initial imaging. Adrenal function should be assessed with a morning cortisol and, if borderline, a cosyntropin stimulation test to rule out acute adrenal insufficiency, which would require immediate glucocorticoid replacement. Conservative management with careful reintroduction of anticoagulation may be appropriate if the patient is hemodynamically stable and adrenal function is preserved.

items.title: Catecholamine-Secreting Retroperitoneal Paraganglioma: A Case Report and Literature Review.
items.summary: This case describes a 75-year-old man with an incidentally discovered 5 cm retroperitoneal paraganglioma confirmed by marked catecholamine hypersecretion and 18F-FDOPA PET/CT. Preoperative alpha-blockade with doxazosin followed by beta-blockade was employed, but intraoperative renal artery injury necessitated en bloc resection including the kidney and ipsilateral adrenal gland. Despite microscopically involved margins, the patient achieved biochemical remission at 6 months; germline testing of a 14-gene PPGL panel was negative, underscoring that a negative panel does not eliminate malignant potential and that lifelong surveillance remains mandatory.
items.caveat: Single case report; microscopically positive margins with only 6-month follow-up means long-term outcomes are unknown. The 14-gene germline panel used may not capture all known susceptibility variants, and Ki-67 <1% does not reliably exclude malignant behavior in paraganglioma.
items.quiz_question: A 68-year-old man has a biochemically active 4.5 cm perihilar retroperitoneal paraganglioma. Germline testing using a 14-gene PPGL panel returns negative. How should this result alter his long-term surveillance plan, and what functional imaging modality is most appropriate for staging?
items.quiz_answer: A negative 14-gene germline panel does not eliminate the risk of malignant behavior or metastatic disease in paraganglioma; lifelong annual clinical and biochemical surveillance (plasma/urinary metanephrines) remains mandatory regardless of genetic results. 18F-FDOPA PET/CT (or 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT depending on tumor biochemistry) is appropriate for functional staging to exclude occult metastatic disease.

items.title: Pediatric Pheochromocytoma With Rapid Cyclic Blood Pressure Fluctuations: A Case Report.
items.summary: This report documents cyclic blood pressure fluctuations — previously described only in adult pheochromocytoma — in a 5-year-old boy with VHL disease and a left adrenal pheochromocytoma. Despite 27 days of titrated doxazosin preoperatively, systolic BP oscillated between 50 and 150 mmHg at ~7-minute intervals immediately after intubation and was refractory to both phenylephrine and phentolamine. Following tumor resection, profound vasoplegic hypotension required triple vasopressor support (norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin) for three days, illustrating the severity of catecholamine withdrawal even with apparently adequate preoperative preparation.
items.caveat: Single pediatric case report; the cyclic pattern's mechanism is not established, and the optimal preoperative alpha-blockade regimen for young children with VHL-associated pheo remains undefined. Generalizability from one case is inherently limited.
items.quiz_question: A 6-year-old girl with confirmed VHL disease is found to have a 2.5 cm left adrenal pheochromocytoma with markedly elevated plasma normetanephrines. She undergoes 4 weeks of doxazosin preoperatively. In the operating room shortly after intubation, her blood pressure begins oscillating between 60 and 160 mmHg every 5–8 minutes independent of surgical stimulation. What is the likely mechanism, and what management challenges should the team anticipate post-resection?
items.quiz_answer: The cyclic BP fluctuations likely reflect episodic autonomous catecholamine release from the tumor, which can be triggered by intubation and is independent of surgical manipulation. These oscillations may be refractory to standard vasopressors and alpha-blockers. After tumor resection, profound vasoplegic hypotension due to abrupt catecholamine withdrawal is expected and may require high-dose multi-agent vasopressor support (norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin) for several days. Anticipatory planning with ICU-level hemodynamic monitoring and vasopressor availability is essential.

items.title: Coexisting adrenal hemangioma and aldosterone-producing micronodule presented as adrenal incidentaloma.
items.summary: This case describes a 67-year-old man with a left adrenal incidentaloma initially showing an equivocal aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) that fluctuated between 115.6 and 52.8 on serial testing, ultimately prompting adrenalectomy after the lesion grew from 1.6 cm to 3.4 cm over three years. Histopathology revealed a cavernous hemangioma, but additional CYP11B2 immunostaining identified a co-existing aldosterone-producing micronodule — confirmed by the marked postoperative ARR normalization to 9.7. The case underscores that adrenal incidentalomas can harbor dual pathologies, and that a single non-diagnostic ARR should not preclude further biochemical surveillance, particularly when imaging suggests a non-adenoma lesion type. Integrated clinicopathological assessment including CYP11B2 staining is essential for complete histological characterization.
items.caveat: Single case report; the equivocal biochemistry could reasonably have led to a watchful-waiting approach rather than surgery, and it is unclear whether the micronodule alone would have caused clinically significant primary aldosteronism.
items.quiz_question: A 67-year-old man has a left adrenal incidentaloma measuring 1.6 cm with an unenhanced CT attenuation of 40 HU. His initial ARR is 115.6, but on repeat testing three years later it is 52.8 with a low-normal aldosterone of 9.5 ng/dL. MRI shows a T2-hyperintense lesion with peripheral nodular enhancement and centripetal filling. How should the dual pathology be identified postoperatively, and what histological marker is key?
items.quiz_answer: After surgical resection, routine H&E confirmed cavernous hemangioma. The co-existing aldosterone-producing micronodule was identified only through CYP11B2 immunohistochemical staining — a marker of aldosterone synthase expression. The dramatic postoperative ARR normalization (to 9.7) provided biochemical corroboration. This case illustrates that CYP11B2 staining should be routinely requested when primary aldosteronism is part of the preoperative differential, even if the dominant lesion appears non-secretory on imaging.

items.title: Case Report: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced hypophysitis presenting as acute paralytic ileus mimicking mechanical bowel obstruction in a patient affected by advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
items.summary: This case reports a 76-year-old man on nivolumab/ipilimumab-based combination therapy who developed profound asthenia, altered mental status, bilious vomiting, and marked gastrointestinal dilation after two cycles — initially prompting surgical consultation for suspected mechanical bowel obstruction. Endocrine evaluation revealed central hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency consistent with ICI-induced hypophysitis; prompt IV hydrocortisone followed by thyroid hormone replacement led to rapid neurological recovery, full restoration of GI motility, and radiological resolution of bowel dilatation, avoiding surgery entirely. A durable partial tumor response persisted for over two years on hormone replacement alone. The case expands the recognized clinical phenotype of ICI hypophysitis to include autonomic-mediated paralytic ileus as a presenting feature.
items.caveat: Single case report; causality between hypophysitis and ileus is strongly supported but not definitively proven — adrenal insufficiency alone could account for the GI dysmotility, and the contribution of hypothyroidism is difficult to disentangle.
items.quiz_question: A 76-year-old man receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab for metastatic NSCLC presents after cycle 2 with fatigue, confusion, bilious vomiting, and CT showing marked gastric and intestinal distension with no transition point. Surgical team is considering exploratory laparotomy. What endocrine evaluation should be urgently obtained, and what is the first-line treatment if hypophysitis is confirmed?
items.quiz_answer: Urgent measurement of morning cortisol (or stimulated cortisol), TSH, free T4, LH, FSH, testosterone (in men), prolactin, and IGF-1 should be obtained. If secondary adrenal insufficiency is confirmed (low cortisol with inappropriately low or normal ACTH), IV hydrocortisone at stress doses should be started immediately — this is life-saving and should not await full workup. In this case, IV hydrocortisone followed by thyroid hormone supplementation resolved the paralytic ileus completely, sparing the patient unnecessary surgery.

items.title: Left ventricular thrombus formation in paraganglioma: a rare but serious complication - a case report.
items.summary: This case describes a 43-year-old man who presented with ischemic necrosis of the left foot due to diffuse arterial thrombosis, in whom echocardiography incidentally revealed a left ventricular thrombus that ultimately led to the diagnosis of an infrarenal paraganglioma confirmed by histology. The authors propose that catecholamine excess from the paraganglioma induced a hypercoagulable state through vasospasm, vascular compression, and direct prothrombotic effects, resulting in thrombi in the lower-extremity arteries, aorta, and left ventricle. Preoperative alpha-blockade and postoperative anticoagulation were central to management. The case highlights that paraganglioma should be on the differential when unexplained thromboembolic disease, especially left ventricular thrombus, is encountered in the absence of obvious cardiomyopathy.
items.caveat: Single case report with limited biochemical detail provided; the precise mechanism linking paraganglioma to left ventricular thrombus formation is speculative, and the infrarenal location is atypical, raising questions about completeness of the diagnostic workup.
items.quiz_question: A 43-year-old man presents with left foot ischemia and necrosis. Imaging reveals diffuse aorto-iliac thrombosis and echocardiography shows a left ventricular thrombus with preserved systolic function. There is no history of atrial fibrillation or hypercoagulable disorder. An infrarenal abdominal mass is incidentally noted. What diagnosis must be urgently excluded, and what is the biochemical first step?
items.quiz_answer: Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma must be urgently excluded given the constellation of unexplained hypercoagulability, hypertensive surges, and an adrenal/para-aortic mass. Biochemical first step is measurement of plasma or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines (or catecholamines). If confirmed, alpha-adrenergic blockade must be established before any surgical intervention to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis.

items.title: Primary adrenal small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma in a patient with sarcoidosis and synchronous colon adenocarcinoma.
items.summary: This case report describes a 76-year-old man with known sarcoidosis found to have an enlarging adrenal incidentaloma that proved to be primary adrenal small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (Ki-67 80%) on laparoscopic adrenalectomy. The diagnostic workup was confounded by coexisting sarcoidosis-related lymphadenopathy that mimicked metastatic disease, underscoring the need for tissue confirmation before attributing lymphadenopathy to a benign cause. The tumor showed partial response to cisplatin/irinotecan, with second-line amrubicin reducing tumor size; comprehensive genomic profiling revealed a tumor mutation burden-high phenotype, which may carry therapeutic implications for checkpoint inhibitor eligibility.
items.caveat: Single case report with inherent limitations in generalizability; management decisions were driven by individual clinical course rather than prospective data. Primary adrenal small cell NEC is exceptionally rare, so evidence-based treatment algorithms do not yet exist.
items.quiz_question: A 74-year-old man with a prior diagnosis of pulmonary sarcoidosis is found to have an adrenal incidentaloma that has grown from 8 mm to 21 mm over 3 years. Post-adrenalectomy pathology shows small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma with Ki-67 of 75%. Follow-up imaging shows new para-aortic lymphadenopathy. What is the most important next step to guide management, and why?
items.quiz_answer: Tissue biopsy of the lymph nodes is essential. As illustrated by this case, sarcoidosis can produce lymphadenopathy that mimics metastatic disease, and assuming malignant spread without pathological confirmation risks inappropriate escalation or under-treatment. CT-guided biopsy confirmed metastatic NEC in this patient, directing appropriate chemotherapy selection.

items.title: Case Report: Veno-Arteriovenous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Management of Pheochromocytoma-Induced Cardiac Arrest in a Post-Partum Patient.
items.summary: A 34-year-old woman, two days post-partum, presented in hypertensive crisis with an 18-cm left adrenal mass suspicious for pheochromocytoma and subsequently suffered cardiac arrest with refractory arrhythmias. She was successfully supported with veno-arteriovenous (V-AV) ECMO — a configuration not previously reported for pheochromocytoma crisis — allowing hemodynamic stabilization prior to uncomplicated adrenal resection. This case adds to the growing literature supporting ECMO as a bridge to surgery in catecholamine-induced cardiogenic shock and highlights the particular peripartum vulnerability period.
items.caveat: Single case report; V-AV ECMO configuration is not yet compared against VA-ECMO in any controlled setting for pheo crisis. The post-partum physiological context may limit direct extrapolation to non-obstetric patients.
items.quiz_question: A 31-year-old woman, 3 days post-partum, develops hypertensive emergency (BP 220/130), flash pulmonary edema, and ventricular fibrillation requiring CPR. CT imaging reveals a large adrenal mass. Standard vasopressors and antiarrhythmics fail to maintain hemodynamic stability. What advanced circulatory support strategy has been reported in this scenario, and what is the rationale for its use?
items.quiz_answer: ECMO — specifically veno-arteriovenous (V-AV) configuration as reported in this case — can be used as a bridge to hemodynamic stabilization and definitive surgical resection. By mechanically supporting both cardiac output and oxygenation during refractory catecholamine-induced arrhythmias and cardiogenic shock, ECMO allows the clinical team to optimize the patient prior to adrenalectomy without the ongoing catecholamine surge destabilizing the patient.

items.title: Pertrochanteric fracture in case of Sheehan syndrome: A rare case report.
items.summary: This case report describes a patient with Sheehan's syndrome who sustained a pertrochanteric hip fracture, illustrating the skeletal fragility that can accompany chronic hypopituitarism — likely driven by GH deficiency, hypogonadism, and secondary hypothyroidism — in the absence of adequate hormone replacement. The patient was managed with proximal femur nail fixation with satisfactory postoperative outcomes. The authors note that no prior case reports have specifically documented this fracture type in the context of Sheehan's syndrome.
items.caveat: Single case report from a developing-country setting where diagnosis may be delayed; no bone density data or fracture risk quantification provided, limiting mechanistic conclusions about which hormonal deficiencies drove bone fragility in this patient.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman from a low-resource setting presents with a low-energy hip fracture. History reveals amenorrhea, failure to lactate, and progressive fatigue after a complicated delivery 5 years prior that required blood transfusions. What unifying diagnosis should be considered, and which hormonal deficiencies are most likely contributing to her skeletal fragility?
items.quiz_answer: Sheehan's syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis) should be strongly considered given the obstetric history and constellation of symptoms. The skeletal fragility in this setting is most likely multifactorial, driven by GH deficiency (reduced bone formation), hypogonadism (accelerated bone resorption), and secondary hypothyroidism, all compounded by delayed diagnosis and absent hormone replacement — as illustrated in this case report.

items.title: New Horizons in Pharmacotherapy for Cushing's Disease and Acromegaly.
items.summary: This review synthesizes the rapidly expanding medical treatment landscape for both Cushing's disease and acromegaly. For Cushing's disease, it highlights individualized selection among newer steroidogenesis inhibitors, pituitary-directed therapies, and glucocorticoid receptor antagonists based on adenoma characteristics, hypercortisolism severity, and patient priorities—with targets extending beyond biochemical normalization to QoL, cardiovascular risk, and durable remission. For acromegaly, it covers newly approved and investigational agents including long-acting subcutaneous octreotide (CAM2029), oral somatostatin receptor agonist paltusotine, extended-interval pasireotide (Debio 4126), allosteric GH receptor antagonists, and direct GH-neutralizing antibodies, framing these within precision medicine and biomarker-guided algorithms.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without systematic methodology or meta-analysis; several agents discussed (e.g., MAR002, CAM4071) remain investigational, and efficacy and safety data from pivotal trials are still maturing.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with confirmed Cushing's disease has persistent hypercortisolism after transsphenoidal surgery. Her adenoma is ACTH-secreting with low somatostatin receptor expression. She has significant metabolic comorbidities including poorly controlled hypertension and glucose intolerance. According to the individualized approach described in this review, which factors should most directly guide selection among steroidogenesis inhibitors, pituitary-directed agents, and glucocorticoid receptor antagonists?
items.quiz_answer: Per the review, therapy selection should be guided by corticotroph adenoma characteristics (e.g., somatostatin receptor expression, tumor size/invasiveness), severity of hypercortisolism, specific comorbidity profile (metabolic, cardiovascular), and patient-specific priorities including QoL and convenience. In this patient with significant metabolic burden and low somatostatin receptor expression, a steroidogenesis inhibitor or glucocorticoid receptor antagonist may be preferred over pituitary-directed somatostatin receptor ligand therapy.

items.title: New and emerging pharmacological treatment options for acromegaly: a 2026 update.
items.summary: This 2026 narrative review catalogs the emerging drug pipeline for acromegaly, detailing six distinct pharmacological classes beyond conventional monthly injectables: a long-acting subcutaneous octreotide depot (CAM2029), the oral selective SST2 agonist paltusotine, an extended-interval pasireotide formulation (Debio 4126), a subcutaneous pasireotide depot (CAM4071), an allosteric GH receptor antagonist (MAR002), and a direct GH-neutralizing antibody. The authors argue that integrating biomarker-guided precision medicine with these agents—offering improved convenience, novel mechanisms, and distinct tolerability profiles—holds significant promise for patients with persistent or uncontrolled disease.
items.caveat: As a narrative review, it is subject to selection bias; several agents are still in early or mid-phase trials without published long-term efficacy or head-to-head comparative data. The precision medicine and biomarker-guided frameworks described remain largely aspirational at this stage.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old man with acromegaly is biochemically uncontrolled on maximum-dose monthly octreotide LAR and is intolerant of pegvisomant due to injection-site reactions. He strongly prefers oral therapy. Based on this 2026 review, which emerging agent would be most appropriate to consider, and what is its mechanism?
items.quiz_answer: Paltusotine, an oral selective somatostatin receptor type 2 (SST2) agonist, is the most relevant emerging option for a patient preferring oral administration. It mimics the mechanism of injectable somatostatin receptor ligands but is administered orally, potentially improving convenience and adherence. Its efficacy in patients with prior injectable SST-RL exposure is an area of ongoing evaluation.

items.title: Pediatric prolactinoma-associated pituitary apoplexy presenting with acute visual loss: a case report, literature review, and management strategy.
items.summary: This case report describes an 11-year-old girl who presented with acute complete right-eye visual loss due to hemorrhagic apoplexy of a prolactinoma (prolactin 987 µg/L). Emergency endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery was performed using a deliberate decompression-first strategy—hematoma evacuation and optic decompression without aggressive capsular dissection—to minimize hypopituitarism risk. Vision was fully restored at extubation, and cabergoline initiated on postoperative day 5 achieved a 93.7% prolactin reduction within 20 days, supporting residual tumor management medically rather than through radical resection.
items.caveat: Single case report with inherent limitations; the 48–54% panhypopituitarism risk cited for gross total resection is drawn from prior literature rather than this series. Multicenter prospective data are explicitly acknowledged as lacking to validate this decompression-first strategy in the pediatric population.
items.quiz_question: An 11-year-old girl presents with acute complete monocular visual loss; MRI shows a hemorrhagic sellar-suprasellar mass and serum prolactin is markedly elevated. Cabergoline is considered but she has acute complete visual loss. What surgical strategy is proposed in this report, and what is the rationale for avoiding gross total resection?
items.quiz_answer: The authors advocate a decompression-first surgical strategy: hematoma evacuation and optic decompression with partial debulking, deliberately avoiding aggressive capsular dissection. The rationale is that gross total resection carries a 48–54% risk of panhypopituitarism in this setting, whereas residual prolactinoma can be effectively managed postoperatively with cabergoline—as demonstrated by the 93.7% prolactin reduction achieved within 20 days in this case.
items.journal: Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM

items.title: Spatial localization patterns in MRI-negative Cushing disease: a comparative pituitary heat map analysis.
items.summary: This retrospective analysis of 153 histologically confirmed corticotroph adenomas (133 MRI-positive, 20 MRI-negative) from a single high-volume surgeon's experience used intraoperative sketches and heat-map spatial analysis to characterize tumor distribution. MRI-positive adenomas preferentially localized to the lateral and dorsal aspects of the anterior pituitary, while MRI-negative adenomas showed no consistent anatomical predilection. MRI-negative patients had significantly higher postoperative nadir cortisol levels, higher reoperation rates (20% vs 3.8%), and a trend toward lower remission (75% vs 91%), underscoring the ongoing surgical challenge in radiographically occult disease.
items.caveat: Single-institution, retrospective series with only 20 MRI-negative cases; all procedures were performed by one highly experienced surgeon (Dr. Oldfield), limiting generalizability. Intraoperative sketch-based documentation introduces annotation subjectivity.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with biochemically confirmed Cushing disease has a negative pituitary MRI and bilateral IPSS lateralization. Based on this heat-map analysis, where in the gland are MRI-positive tumors more likely to cluster, and what does this imply for surgical exploration of MRI-negative cases?
items.quiz_answer: MRI-positive corticotroph adenomas more frequently localize to the lateral and dorsal anterior pituitary. MRI-negative adenomas lack a consistent spatial predilection, so surgical exploration cannot be reliably directed by anatomical probability alone—intraoperative findings and individual anatomy must guide the approach, and reoperation rates remain substantially higher in this group.

items.title: Cabergoline for non-functioning pituitary adenomas: an update on an old clinical controversy.
items.summary: This focused narrative review synthesizes evidence through September 2026 on off-label cabergoline use for NFPAs, concluding that the data remain inconsistent and insufficient to support routine use. The only randomized open-label trial showed a radiological signal (less growth, more shrinkage) but no established patient-centered benefit; a 2022 multicenter study found no clear advantage over observation, and a 2024 surgery-naive cohort showed shrinkage/stability/growth rates of 20%/48%/32%. The authors emphasize that contemporary natural-history data show untreated NFPAs can behave unpredictably, making it difficult to attribute radiological stability to drug effect.
items.caveat: Evidence synthesis is narrative rather than meta-analytic, and the randomized trial reviewed was open-label. No validated molecular predictor of cabergoline response has emerged, so patient selection remains empirical. Authors' conclusion against routine use may evolve with ongoing prospective data.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old man has a 12 mm incidental non-functioning pituitary adenoma with no mass effect. A colleague suggests starting cabergoline to prevent growth. How does the current evidence base support or refute this approach?
items.quiz_answer: Current evidence does not support routine cabergoline for NFPAs. The only randomized trial showed primarily a radiological signal without established patient-centered benefit, a 2022 multicenter comparison found no clear advantage over observation alone, and no molecular predictor of response exists. Cabergoline remains off-label and should not displace standard surveillance, with neurosurgical or radiotherapy options reserved for lesions with mass effect or documented growth.

items.title: 68Ga-Pentixafor PET/MRI for identifying corticotroph adenomas in Cushing disease: a pilot study.
items.summary: This single-center pilot enrolled 10 patients with confirmed Cushing disease (5 newly diagnosed, 5 persistent/recurrent) to evaluate CXCR4-targeted 68Ga-Pentixafor PET/MRI. Only 2 of 10 scans showed focal pituitary uptake, one of which correlated with confirmed remission; the other had negative pathology and persistent postoperative disease despite IPSS centralization. Three patients with negative scans achieved remission after surgery, confirming false-negative imaging, and the overall performance was limited and variable.
items.caveat: Extremely small sample (n=10) with heterogeneous disease states (newly diagnosed vs. persistent/recurrent); no head-to-head comparison with standard MRI protocols or other novel tracers. Results are insufficient to alter diagnostic algorithms or replace IPSS.
items.quiz_question: A 44-year-old woman with ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome has a negative 3T pituitary MRI. Her IPSS confirms central ACTH secretion. A colleague proposes 68Ga-Pentixafor PET/MRI before surgery. What does current evidence suggest about this approach?
items.quiz_answer: Based on this pilot, 68Ga-Pentixafor PET/MRI showed limited and variable performance, with false-negative results even in surgically confirmed cases. It is not yet ready for incorporation into diagnostic algorithms and should not be considered an alternative to IPSS. It may provide complementary information in selected patients with equivocal MRI findings, but the evidence base is insufficient to justify routine use.

items.title: Prevalence of Mild Autonomous Cortisol Secretion Among Patients With Adrenal Incidentaloma and Its Association With Metabolic Abnormalities: A Hospital-Based, Analytical, Cross-Sectional Study.
items.summary: In a cross-sectional study of 380 adults with adrenal incidentaloma at a Pakistani tertiary center, MACS (defined by 1-mg overnight DST) was identified in 25% of patients. After multivariable adjustment, MACS was independently associated with obesity (aOR 1.85), diabetes mellitus (aOR 1.68), and metabolic syndrome (aOR 1.82), with larger lesion size also independently predicting MACS (aOR 1.38 per cm). These findings reinforce current guidelines advocating routine cortisol secretion assessment in incidentaloma patients given the associated cardiometabolic burden.
items.caveat: Single-center, cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; the Pakistani hospital-based sample may not be generalizable, and the study cannot determine whether MACS predates or drives the observed metabolic abnormalities.
items.quiz_question: A 54-year-old woman is referred after a 3.2 cm right adrenal incidentaloma is found on CT for abdominal pain. She has hypertension and central obesity but no frank Cushingoid features. Based on findings from this study, what is the approximate prevalence of MACS in this clinical scenario, and what single screening test should you prioritize?
items.quiz_answer: Approximately 25% of adrenal incidentaloma patients harbor MACS in this population. The 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) is the recommended screening test; post-DST cortisol ≥1.8 µg/dL warrants further evaluation, particularly given her coexisting metabolic risk factors.

items.title: Diagnostic challenges of masked arginine vasopressin deficiency in neurosarcoidosis complicated by sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor use.
items.summary: This case report describes an 82-year-old man with hypothalamic-pituitary sarcoidosis who developed arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) whose hallmark hypotonic polyuria was masked by concurrent adrenal insufficiency, CKD, and SGLT2 inhibitor use — the latter independently driving glucosuria-related osmotic diuresis and urine output. The diagnosis was only appreciated after glucocorticoid replacement unmasked the AVP-D. As SGLT2 inhibitor prescribing grows broadly, this interaction represents a clinically underappreciated confounder when evaluating water balance in patients with hypothalamic-pituitary disease.
items.caveat: Single case report; causal attribution of symptom masking to the SGLT2 inhibitor versus CKD versus adrenal insufficiency alone cannot be formally disentangled.
items.quiz_question: A 75-year-old man with pituitary sarcoidosis, CKD stage 3, and type 2 diabetes on empagliflozin is started on hydrocortisone for newly confirmed secondary adrenal insufficiency. Two months later he reports increasing thirst and nocturia but no dramatic polyuria. Serum sodium is 143 mEq/L. What diagnostic pitfall does this case highlight, and how should you proceed?
items.quiz_answer: SGLT2 inhibitors cause osmotic diuresis that can obscure the hypotonic polyuria characteristic of AVP-D, and CKD further limits maximal urine dilution. Despite the absence of florid polyuria, AVP-D should be actively considered. Temporarily discontinuing the SGLT2 inhibitor, checking urine and serum osmolality, and performing a careful water deprivation assessment (or copeptin-based testing) would be appropriate next steps.

items.title: Pituitary Apoplexy Presenting as a Transient Ischemic Attack: An Endocrine Emergency.
items.summary: This case illustrates pituitary apoplexy presenting as apparent TIA (dysarthria, right upper limb weakness, NIHSS 3) in a 67-year-old man with significant carotid stenosis, where the focal deficits resolved with fluid resuscitation and hydrocortisone rather than with TIA management. Cortisol was <1 µg/dL with inappropriately low ACTH, confirming acute secondary adrenal insufficiency as the hemodynamic driver superimposed on fixed vascular disease. Antiplatelet therapy initiated empirically for presumed stroke was appropriately withdrawn once MRI confirmed hemorrhagic pituitary macroadenoma.
items.caveat: Single case report; the co-presence of 90% carotid stenosis introduces genuine diagnostic ambiguity and limits generalizability, though the hemodynamic resolution with steroids is mechanistically compelling.
items.quiz_question: A 64-year-old man with known carotid artery disease presents with sudden-onset left arm weakness and dysarthria that fully resolve within 30 minutes, along with persistent hypotension unresponsive to 2L IV saline. Random cortisol returns at 0.8 µg/dL. What is the critical next step before initiating antiplatelet therapy?
items.quiz_answer: Administer empirical stress-dose hydrocortisone immediately without waiting for confirmatory testing, then obtain emergent pituitary MRI to evaluate for pituitary apoplexy. If hemorrhagic macroadenoma is confirmed, antiplatelet therapy should be withheld, as the neurological event was likely hemodynamic (apoplexy-driven adrenal insufficiency causing hypotension on background vascular disease) rather than thromboembolic.

items.title: Growth hormone-releasing hormone-secreting giant pheochromocytoma causing acromegaly: a case report with a review of the literature.
items.summary: This case describes a 57-year-old woman with a large left pheochromocytoma who presented with acromegaloid features (enlarged nose and lips, macroglossia) and biochemically confirmed GH excess on oral glucose tolerance testing, yet had only a mildly enlarged pituitary gland with no discrete tumor on MRI. Left adrenalectomy normalized GH excess, and immunohistochemistry of the resected tumor confirmed GHRH secretion—establishing a diagnosis of ectopic acromegaly from a GHRH-secreting PPGL, an entity representing well under 1% of acromegaly cases. The case reinforces that thorough physical examination is indispensable in PPGL workup, and that a structurally unremarkable pituitary does not exclude acromegaly when an ectopic source is present.
items.caveat: Single case report; cannot establish prevalence or generalize management. Ectopic GHRH acromegaly from PPGLs remains so rare that systematic evidence on optimal perioperative management is essentially absent.
items.quiz_question: A 60-year-old woman with a known right adrenal mass presents with progressive coarsening of facial features over 3 years. IGF-1 is elevated and GH fails to suppress on 75 g OGTT. Pituitary MRI shows diffuse mild gland enlargement but no discrete adenoma. What is the next most important diagnostic and management step?
items.quiz_answer: Measure plasma or urine GHRH levels and pursue functional imaging (e.g., MIBG, somatostatin receptor scintigraphy or DOTATATE PET) to confirm ectopic GHRH secretion from the adrenal mass. Resection of the PPGL after appropriate alpha-blockade is the definitive treatment and should normalize GH/IGF-1 if the adrenal tumor is the source.

items.title: Higher ARNT expression is associated with the sparsely granulated phenotype in somatotroph pituitary adenomas: An immunohistochemical study.
items.summary: In a retrospective series of 71 surgically treated somatotroph adenomas, moderate-to-strong ARNT (aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator) immunoexpression was significantly more frequent in sparsely granulated (SG) than densely granulated (DG) tumors (60% vs. 18%; adjusted OR 6.84), and ARNT-high patients were younger (median 39 vs. 46 years). However, ARNT expression did not associate with Ki-67 index, baseline GH or IGF-1 levels, or biochemical response to first-generation somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs), suggesting it reflects granulation-pattern differentiation rather than independent prognostic biology. The authors appropriately conclude that ARNT adds no actionable prognostic or therapeutic information beyond granulation pattern itself at this stage.
items.caveat: Retrospective, single-center design with only 71 patients; granulation pattern was already known to predict SRL response, so ARNT adds limited incremental value with current data. No functional or transcriptomic validation was performed.
items.quiz_question: A 39-year-old patient undergoes transsphenoidal resection of a somatotroph adenoma. Pathology returns a sparsely granulated tumor with strong ARNT immunostaining and a Ki-67 of 1.5%. How should ARNT expression alter your postoperative management plan compared to standard SG adenoma follow-up?
items.quiz_answer: Based on current evidence, ARNT expression should not change management. The sparsely granulated phenotype itself already predicts poorer SRL response, and this study found no independent association between ARNT expression and Ki-67, GH/IGF-1 levels, or SRL biochemical control. Standard SG adenoma surveillance and consideration of pegvisomant or combination therapy for biochemical non-responders applies regardless of ARNT status.

items.title: Biogenic amines as neuroendocrine tumor markers: limitations and future perspectives.
items.summary: This review critically evaluates the evolution of biogenic amine testing for catecholamine-producing tumors (pheochromocytoma, paraganglioma, neuroblastoma), highlighting the shift from immunoassay-based methods to LC-MS/MS platforms that offer superior sensitivity and multiplexing capability. The authors emphasize that dopamine-derived 3-methoxytyramine (3-MT) is gaining clinical importance as a marker associated with MYCN-amplified tumor biology and worse outcomes in neuroblastoma and selected paraganglioma subtypes. Despite these advances, the absence of full metrological traceability and inter-laboratory harmonization continues to limit clinically meaningful comparisons of results across centers.
items.caveat: Review article without new primary data; emphasis on 3-MT in paraganglioma subtypes is based on emerging rather than practice-validated evidence, and LC-MS/MS is not yet universally available. Inter-laboratory variability remains an unresolved practical barrier.
items.quiz_question: You receive a plasma metanephrine panel on a patient with a suspected dopaminergic paraganglioma: normetanephrine and metanephrine are only mildly elevated, but 3-methoxytyramine (3-MT) is markedly elevated. What is the clinical significance of the 3-MT elevation, and how does it inform further workup?
items.quiz_answer: Marked 3-MT elevation points toward a predominantly dopamine-secreting tumor, which is more commonly associated with extra-adrenal paraganglioma (especially head/neck or thoracoabdominal) and with SDHB or MYCN-related genetic subtypes that carry higher malignant potential. This finding should prompt functional imaging (DOTATATE PET preferred) and germline genetic testing, particularly for SDH mutations, given the elevated risk of metastatic disease in this biochemical phenotype.

items.title: Hair cortisol as a complementary marker of chronic glucocorticoid exposure in mild autonomous cortisol secretion.
items.summary: This cross-sectional study compared hair cortisol concentrations (HCC) in 73 patients with mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) versus 60 healthy controls, finding significantly elevated HCC in MACS (median 3.6 vs. 1.75 ng/g; p<0.01). HCC correlated modestly with waist circumference and late-night salivary cortisol, but not with DST-based measures or urinary free cortisol. However, ROC analysis demonstrated only modest discrimination (AUC 0.60), and after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI, HCC was not independently associated with MACS. The authors conclude HCC may serve as a complementary—but not standalone—biomarker of cumulative glucocorticoid exposure in adrenal incidentaloma workup.
items.caveat: Cross-sectional design, modest sample size, and failure to achieve independent association after multivariable adjustment temper enthusiasm; HCC is not yet ready for routine clinical use in MACS evaluation. Hair growth rate variability and confounders such as hair treatments were not fully addressed.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman with a 2.2 cm adrenal incidentaloma has post-1 mg DST cortisol of 2.1 µg/dL (marginally elevated), normal 24h UFC, and borderline late-night salivary cortisol. You consider hair cortisol concentration to assess cumulative exposure. Based on this study, what is the most accurate characterization of HCC's diagnostic utility in this scenario?
items.quiz_answer: HCC is modestly elevated in MACS patients compared to controls and may add complementary information about chronic glucocorticoid exposure, but its diagnostic performance is limited (AUC ~0.60) and it is not independently associated with MACS after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI. It should be used as an adjunct to—not a replacement for—conventional HPA axis testing.

items.title: Oncological Outcomes and Safety Profiles of Adjuvant Nivolumab in Muscle-Invasive Urothelial Carcinoma.
items.summary: In this multicenter real-world cohort of 97 patients receiving adjuvant nivolumab for muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma, immune-related adrenal insufficiency and hypophysitis occurred in 8% and 4% of patients, respectively—rates the authors note appear higher than those reported in pivotal trial data. Grade ≥3 endocrine irAEs presented between 3.3 and 18.3 months after initiating therapy, emphasizing the prolonged surveillance window required. Clinicians are reminded that nonspecific symptoms and considerable timing variability make these diagnoses easy to miss without proactive biochemical monitoring.
items.caveat: Retrospective multicenter real-world study without a standardized endocrine screening protocol, so ascertainment bias likely inflates or distorts irAE rates compared to prospectively monitored trials. Small sample size (n=97) limits precise incidence estimates.
items.quiz_question: A 67-year-old man on adjuvant nivolumab after radical cystectomy for pT3 bladder cancer presents at month 14 with fatigue, nausea, and a blood pressure of 92/60 mmHg. Morning cortisol returns at 3.2 µg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis and what is the appropriate immediate management?
items.quiz_answer: This presentation is consistent with checkpoint inhibitor-induced adrenal insufficiency (irAE), which this study found in 8% of nivolumab-treated patients with onset ranging beyond 3 months. Immediate management includes stress-dose IV hydrocortisone (100 mg bolus followed by infusion or q6-8h dosing), IV fluid resuscitation, and hospital admission. Long-term oral hydrocortisone ± fludrocortisone will be required, and nivolumab should be held pending endocrinology evaluation.
items.journal: International journal of urology : official journal of the Japanese Urological Association

items.title: Pembrolizumab-Associated Adrenal Insufficiency Presenting as Adrenal Crisis: A Case Report.
items.summary: This case report describes an adrenal crisis occurring 12 days after completion of a full 24-month pembrolizumab course in a man with metastatic NSCLC. Routine outpatient labs first flagged critical hypocortisolemia (morning cortisol <50 nmol/L) before the patient developed severe hypotension and GI symptoms; he was successfully resuscitated with IV fluids and high-dose hydrocortisone and ultimately transitioned to maintenance hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone. The case reinforces that checkpoint inhibitor-related adrenal insufficiency can manifest abruptly even after treatment completion, with no temporal ceiling on risk.
items.caveat: Single case report; causality cannot be rigorously established, and the contribution of underlying metastatic disease or other medications to adrenal dysfunction cannot be excluded. Evidence level is low by design.
items.quiz_question: A patient with NSCLC completed a planned 24-month course of pembrolizumab two weeks ago and now presents to the ED with hypotension, nausea, and vomiting. Sepsis workup is unrevealing. What endocrine diagnosis must be urgently considered, and what biochemical test should be ordered immediately?
items.quiz_answer: Pembrolizumab-associated adrenal insufficiency presenting as adrenal crisis should be urgently considered, as this case illustrates it can occur even shortly after treatment completion. A random (or morning) serum cortisol should be drawn immediately; if critically low or clinical suspicion is high, empirical IV hydrocortisone should be administered without waiting for results. An ACTH level drawn concurrently will help characterize primary versus secondary etiology.

items.title: Pediatric sellar and parasellar lesions: a population-based cohort study of presentation, management, and endocrine outcomes.
items.summary: This retrospective population-based cohort (n=104, diagnosed 1976–2021) found that endocrine dysfunction at presentation was significantly more common with sellar/parasellar lesions ≥10 mm than <10 mm (74% vs. 49%), and post-treatment endocrine morbidity was strikingly higher in the larger-lesion group (65% vs. 13%). Importantly, clinically relevant endocrine abnormalities also occurred in smaller lesions, supporting routine endocrine evaluation regardless of lesion size. Pituitary adenomas carried the highest burden of endocrine abnormality at diagnosis among lesion subtypes.
items.caveat: Retrospective design spanning nearly five decades introduces significant heterogeneity in diagnostic and management practices. Associations with treatment modality are descriptive and subject to confounding by indication. Single-region population limits generalizability.
items.quiz_question: A 12-year-old presents with a 7 mm incidentally found sellar lesion on MRI done for headaches. Based on this population-based cohort, is endocrine evaluation warranted, and what does the data suggest about smaller lesions?
items.quiz_answer: Yes, endocrine evaluation is warranted. Although endocrine dysfunction was less frequent with lesions <10 mm, nearly half (49%) still had abnormalities at presentation, and clinically relevant dysfunction occurred even in smaller lesions. The authors explicitly support endocrine evaluation based on clinical context and longitudinal surveillance, regardless of lesion size.

items.title: Structured Physiotherapy Improves Functional Outcomes in Acromegalic Arthropathy After Biochemical Remission: A Prospective Controlled Study.
items.summary: In this prospective controlled study of 13 acromegaly patients in biochemical remission, a standardized 15-session knee-focused physiotherapy program produced clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function: 85% met the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) threshold for BPI and 100% for WOMAC Total. However, joint stiffness showed limited responsiveness, and pretreatment IGF-1 correlated strongly negatively with stiffness improvement (r = −0.77), suggesting stiffness is more structurally driven and less reversible. Higher BMI predicted better pain/BPI improvement but worse WOMAC Total improvement.
items.caveat: Very small sample size (n=13 per group) limits statistical power and generalizability. The control group had greater baseline severity, which complicates direct comparison of response magnitude. No long-term follow-up data beyond the intervention period are reported.
items.quiz_question: A 48-year-old woman with acromegaly in biochemical remission for 2 years continues to report significant knee pain and stiffness. Which domain of musculoskeletal symptoms is least likely to respond to a structured physiotherapy program based on this study, and what biomarker correlates with this limited response?
items.quiz_answer: Joint stiffness is the domain least likely to respond to physiotherapy in acromegaly patients in remission, as it showed limited responsiveness compared to pain and function. Pretreatment IGF-1 correlated strongly negatively with stiffness improvement (r = −0.77), suggesting residual stiffness reflects structural joint changes rather than reversible inflammation.

items.title: Endocrine therapies and hormonal dysfunction after traumatic brain injury: A scoping review.
items.summary: This scoping review of 67 studies found post-traumatic endocrine dysfunction to be common and heterogeneous, with GH deficiency being the most frequently reported deficiency after TBI; both hypoprolactinemia and hyperprolactinemia were also identified as underappreciated contributors to post-TBI metabolic morbidity. GH replacement therapy showed improvements in cognition, fatigue, mood, and quality of life in several studies, though effects on functional outcomes and mortality were inconsistent. Progesterone failed to demonstrate efficacy in large RCTs despite early promise, with timing of initiation appearing critical.
items.caveat: Scoping reviews do not perform meta-analysis or formal quality appraisal, so conclusions on therapeutic efficacy are limited. Study heterogeneity in TBI severity classification, endocrine testing protocols, and timing of assessment makes cross-study comparisons difficult. Evidence base remains dominated by small, underpowered trials.
items.quiz_question: A 35-year-old male presents 18 months after moderate TBI with persistent fatigue, cognitive slowing, and low libido. Screening reveals low IGF-1 and an inadequate GH response to stimulation testing. What does the current evidence base suggest regarding GH replacement in this population, and what caveat should guide your counseling?
items.quiz_answer: GH replacement after TBI-related GH deficiency has shown improvements in cognition, fatigue, mood, and quality of life in several studies reviewed. However, effects on functional outcomes and mortality are inconsistent, study designs are highly heterogeneous, and sample sizes are generally small. Patients should be counseled that evidence is promising but not yet definitive, and that larger, well-designed trials are still needed.
items.journal: Growth hormone & IGF research : official journal of the Growth Hormone Research Society and the International IGF Research Society

items.title: Adrenal Collision Tumors: A Practical Application of the Existing Evidence.
items.summary: This narrative review tackles a practical pitfall in adrenal incidentaloma workup: collision tumors (two histologically distinct lesions in the same gland) render the standard CT washout protocol unreliable, potentially mimicking malignancy. The authors argue that the established incidentaloma pathway—biochemical exclusion of pheochromocytoma and adrenocortical carcinoma, followed by imaging phenotyping and size/growth-based surveillance—remains the correct framework and can reliably identify both functional and malignant components without reflexive surgery. The key clinical message is that the radiologic complexity of collision tumors should not override a structured risk-stratification approach.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review drawing on institutional experience and case literature, not a prospective cohort or systematic review, so the evidence base is inherently limited and subject to publication bias toward unusual cases.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman has an adrenal incidentaloma with a heterogeneous CT appearance: one region has density <10 HU and another region has soft-tissue density that does not washout appropriately. Biochemical workup is negative for pheochromocytoma and hypercortisolism. What is the most important caveat when interpreting the CT washout data, and what is the recommended next step?
items.quiz_answer: In an adrenal collision tumor, the mixed composition of the lesion renders CT washout calculations unreliable—the lipid-poor component will dilute washout percentages and can falsely suggest malignancy. The recommended approach is to continue the standard incidentaloma pathway: confirm biochemical exclusion of pheochromocytoma and adrenocortical carcinoma, consider alternative imaging (e.g., MRI with chemical shift or FDG-PET) for further phenotyping, and apply size- and growth-based surveillance rather than proceeding directly to surgery based on washout failure alone.
items.journal: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists

items.title: From Trauma to Tumour: Incidental Giant Left Adrenal Myelolipoma in Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia.
items.summary: This case report describes a 49-year-old woman with known CAH in whom a 12 cm adrenal myelolipoma was incidentally discovered on trauma CT, highlighting that chronic ACTH hypersecretion from suboptimal glucocorticoid control is the principal driver of myelolipoma development in CAH. Despite reported adherence to hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, persistently elevated adrenal steroid precursors and renin confirmed inadequate control. The patient was referred for adrenalectomy given size >10 cm and hemorrhage risk, reinforcing that rigorous biochemical monitoring and periodic adrenal imaging should be considered in CAH patients.
items.caveat: Single case report; no systematic data on optimal surveillance imaging intervals or size thresholds for surgery in CAH-associated myelolipoma. The hemorrhage risk at >10 cm is extrapolated from sporadic myelolipoma literature rather than CAH-specific evidence.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old man with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone presents for routine follow-up. His 17-OHP is markedly elevated and renin is elevated. Abdominal imaging for an unrelated indication reveals a 7 cm left adrenal lesion with macroscopic fat on CT, consistent with myelolipoma. What is the most likely pathophysiological driver of myelolipoma formation in this patient, and what management change should be prioritized?
items.quiz_answer: Chronic ACTH hypersecretion secondary to inadequate cortisol replacement is the principal driver of myelolipoma formation in CAH. The immediate priority is optimization of glucocorticoid (and mineralocorticoid) replacement to suppress ACTH, as evidenced by the elevated 17-OHP and renin indicating suboptimal control. For the lesion itself, given its size of 7 cm (below the >10 cm threshold where hemorrhage risk is highest), continued surveillance with imaging is reasonable while optimizing medical therapy, though multidisciplinary review is warranted.

items.title: When Appearances Deceive: A Silent Somatotroph Macroadenoma Presenting With Acromegaloid Features and Paradoxically Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1.
items.summary: This case illustrates a diagnostic trap: a 32-year-old man had classic acromegaloid phenotype (frontal bossing, spade hands, coarse facies) with a giant invasive sellar mass, yet preoperative IGF-1 was paradoxically below the reference range. Neuropathology confirmed a densely granulated PIT1-lineage somatotroph adenoma with GH immunopositivity and Ki-67 <2%, representing a silent somatotroph adenoma. The authors emphasize that clinical-biochemical discordance in the setting of a pituitary mass mandates histopathological and immunohistochemical confirmation, and that silent somatotroph adenomas carry risk of eventual phenotypic conversion to functioning acromegaly requiring long-term surveillance.
items.caveat: Single case report; the mechanism for low IGF-1 despite GH-immunopositive tumor (possibly aberrant GH isoforms or receptor insensitivity) is speculative and not biochemically characterized in this report. Generalizability is limited.
items.quiz_question: A 35-year-old woman presents with enlarging hands, jaw protrusion, and a 3 cm invasive pituitary macroadenoma on MRI. Her random GH is mildly elevated but IGF-1 is below the lower limit of normal. How should you interpret this clinical-biochemical discordance, and what is the key diagnostic step after surgical resection?
items.quiz_answer: This pattern should raise suspicion for a silent somatotroph adenoma—a PIT1-lineage tumor that immunohistochemically expresses GH but does not produce the full biochemical syndrome of acromegaly. IGF-1 alone is insufficient to exclude or confirm the diagnosis in this context. The key post-resection step is histopathological analysis with GH and Pit-1 immunohistochemistry; confirmation of a silent somatotroph adenoma mandates long-term neuroendocrine and neurosurgical surveillance given the potential for phenotypic transformation to overt acromegaly.

items.title: Polygenic risk score identifies alternative etiologies in misdiagnosed cases of primary adrenal insufficiency.
items.summary: This study applied a polygenic risk score for autoimmune Addison's disease (PRS14AAD) to 124 seronegative patients diagnosed with autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI). Among those with low PRS14AAD, 41% were ultimately re-diagnosed with non-autoimmune etiologies — including monogenic PAI (17%) and infectious/non-primary causes (23%). Crucially, four of six confirmed monogenic cases presented with adult-onset disease, underscoring that late-onset monogenic PAI is more common than traditionally appreciated. The authors conclude that genetic evaluation should be considered in all seronegative PAI patients, regardless of age at diagnosis.
items.caveat: Sample sizes in the re-evaluated subgroups are small (n=35 low-PRS, n=10 high-PRS), and this is a single-center study design without prospective validation of the PRS14AAD in routine clinical workflows. The 7 patients carrying 'suspected' monogenic variants without confirmation add interpretive uncertainty.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency. Her 21-hydroxylase antibodies are negative. She has no family history and no clinical features of tuberculosis. Based on the findings of this study, what next step would be most informative in determining her etiology?
items.quiz_answer: Calculation of a polygenic risk score for autoimmune Addison's disease (PRS14AAD) can stratify her likelihood of truly having autoimmune PAI. If her PRS14AAD is low, she has a substantially higher probability of a non-autoimmune etiology — including a monogenic cause — and whole-genome or targeted genetic sequencing should be pursued regardless of her adult age at diagnosis.

items.title: Imaging features of pituitary Crooke cell adenoma: a 13-case series.
items.summary: This retrospective series of 13 Crooke cell adenomas (CCAs) characterizes their MRI features, finding that most macroadenomas are T2-hyperintense while most microadenomas are T2-hypointense — a size-dependent signal pattern potentially useful for preoperative suspicion. Mild contrast enhancement was the dominant enhancement pattern (77% of cases), and Knosp grade 1 was the most frequent parasellar extension. Of particular clinical note, all four patients who experienced postoperative tumor progression shared a finding of reduced enhancement of the tumor-adjacent internal carotid artery wall on preoperative MRI, raising the possibility that this may be a prognostic imaging marker.
items.caveat: The series is small (n=13), retrospective, and single-center, with follow-up as short as 2 months in some cases. The ICA wall enhancement finding as a progression predictor is hypothesis-generating only and explicitly requires validation in larger cohorts — the authors themselves caution this.
items.quiz_question: A patient with Cushing's disease undergoes transsphenoidal surgery. Pathology returns as Crooke cell adenoma (CCA) after subtotal resection. Which preoperative MRI finding, described in this series, may have predicted the higher risk of postoperative tumor progression in this patient?
items.quiz_answer: Reduced contrast enhancement of the tumor-adjacent internal carotid artery wall (ICAW) on preoperative MRI was observed in all four patients who developed postoperative tumor progression in this series. Recognizing this finding in the preoperative workup of CCA patients undergoing subtotal resection may warrant closer surveillance, though the finding requires validation in larger prospective studies.

items.title: Neuroendocrine dysfunction after TBI: A guide for the clinical neuropsychologist.
items.summary: This review synthesizes current evidence on post-traumatic hypopituitarism (PTHP) following traumatic brain injury, highlighting that a high proportion of moderate-to-severe TBI cases develop pituitary dysfunction, with GH deficiency being the most prevalent. Notably, the review presents emerging evidence that individuals with persistent symptoms after mild TBI may develop neuroendocrine dysfunction at rates comparable to moderate-to-severe TBI. The review also discusses how hormonal dysregulation — as well as metabolic disturbances including altered gut microbiota and amino acid imbalances — may compound cognitive impairment and fatigue, underscoring the need for pituitary screening in this population.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without meta-analytic methodology, and many of the cited studies are heterogeneous in TBI severity classification, timing of hormonal testing, and diagnostic thresholds for pituitary dysfunction. The mild TBI/PTHP evidence base is particularly limited, and causal attribution is difficult given overlapping psychiatric comorbidities.
items.quiz_question: A 34-year-old man presents 18 months after a mild TBI with persistent fatigue, cognitive slowing, and low mood despite normal neuroimaging and psychiatric treatment. He was never screened for pituitary dysfunction. According to the evidence reviewed, what is the most common hormonal deficiency to screen for in this setting, and why is it clinically significant?
