items.quiz_answer: Growth hormone deficiency (GHD) is the most prevalent form of post-traumatic hypopituitarism across TBI severity categories. It is clinically significant because GHD can directly contribute to fatigue, impaired cognition, and mood disturbance — symptoms frequently attributed solely to post-concussive syndrome — and targeted GH replacement may improve outcomes if deficiency is confirmed.

items.title: Postpartum diagnosis of pheochromocytoma presenting as atypical hypertensive disorder of pregnancy: A case report.
items.summary: This case describes a 29-year-old primigravida managed as pre-eclampsia from 34–36 weeks gestation whose postpartum course of labile hypertension, paroxysmal headaches, tachycardia, and diaphoresis triggered biochemical and imaging workup revealing a 4 cm right adrenal pheochromocytoma confirmed by markedly elevated plasma and urinary normetanephrines. Right adrenalectomy seven weeks postpartum resulted in complete symptom resolution, and subsequent surveillance showed no recurrence. A second uncomplicated pregnancy followed, underscoring the value of thorough multidisciplinary management once the diagnosis is secured.
items.caveat: Single case report; no systematic data on how frequently pheo masquerades as pre-eclampsia or on optimal alpha-blockade timing postpartum. Gestational diabetes was also present, which can itself confound the clinical picture.
items.quiz_question: A 29-year-old woman is managed postpartum for persistent labile hypertension, paroxysmal headaches, and diaphoresis after a pregnancy complicated by apparent pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes. What biochemical tests should be prioritized next, and what finding would most strongly support pheochromocytoma over residual pregnancy-related hypertension?
items.quiz_answer: Plasma free metanephrines and 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines should be ordered. Markedly elevated normetanephrines (as seen in this case) in the postpartum setting, combined with paroxysmal symptoms, are highly specific for pheochromocytoma and distinguish it from typical postpartum hypertension. Adrenal imaging should follow biochemical confirmation.

items.title: Tumor-to-tumor metastasis of colorectal adenocarcinoma within a gonadotroph pituitary adenoma.
items.summary: A 66-year-old man with metastatic sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma on FOLFOX6 plus panitumumab had a sellar mass that grew slowly over two years despite controlled extracranial disease. Transsphenoidal resection demonstrated a gonadotroph pituitary adenoma infiltrated throughout by colorectal adenocarcinoma—favoring true tumor-to-tumor metastasis rather than a collision tumor—with viable cancer cells showing no treatment effect from prolonged chemotherapy. The case reinforces that sellar mass enlargement in a patient with a known primary malignancy warrants tissue diagnosis even when the radiologic appearance suggests adenoma.
items.caveat: Single case report; the histologic distinction between tumor-to-tumor metastasis and a collision tumor is inherently observer-dependent. The rarity of colorectal pituitary metastases limits generalizability to other primaries.
items.quiz_question: A 66-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer on systemic chemotherapy has a sellar mass radiologically consistent with a pituitary adenoma that slowly enlarges over 24 months despite good systemic disease control. What is the most important next step, and what unexpected finding should be on your differential?
items.quiz_answer: Transsphenoidal biopsy/resection is indicated for diagnostic certainty. The differential must include pituitary metastasis or—as illustrated in this report—tumor-to-tumor metastasis of the colorectal adenocarcinoma into a pre-existing gonadotroph adenoma. A sellar mass that grows despite effective systemic therapy should not be assumed to be a benign adenoma without histopathologic confirmation.

items.title: GNAI2 activating variants and MAGIS syndrome: long-term endocrine and growth outcome.
items.summary: This report characterizes longitudinal endocrine outcomes in a child with MAGIS syndrome (midline brain malformations, anterior pituitary dysfunction, growth retardation, immunodysregulation, skeletal defects) caused by a de novo GNAI2 p.Thr182Pro variant. Despite recombinant GH therapy, the patient showed suboptimal height velocity with persistently low IGF-1, and developed progressive deficiencies in prolactin and gonadotropins over time, alongside immune dysregulation. The authors highlight that MAGIS syndrome involves a more complex and evolving hypopituitarism phenotype than initially recognized, warranting regular reassessment of all pituitary axes.
items.caveat: Single patient case with review; MAGIS syndrome itself was only recently described, so the full spectrum of endocrine phenotypes and GH responsiveness remains poorly characterized. No comparative data are available to guide treatment targets.
items.quiz_question: A 9-year-old male with a known de novo GNAI2 activating variant, anterior pituitary hypoplasia on MRI, and short stature is on recombinant GH therapy but shows persistently low IGF-1 and suboptimal height velocity. What additional pituitary axes should be monitored closely over time, and why?
items.quiz_answer: Based on this MAGIS syndrome case, prolactin, gonadotropins (LH/FSH), and thyroid axis (central hypothyroidism) should all be monitored longitudinally, as the endocrine phenotype appears progressive. The evolving deficiencies in this case illustrate that initial hormonal assessments may underestimate the full degree of hypopituitarism, and regular re-evaluation is essential.

items.title: Machine learning quantifies within-subject facial change in acromegaly.
items.summary: In this multicenter international cohort study, a face-recognition machine-learning model was able to detect measurable within-person facial shifts toward an acromegaly-associated pattern over time, with 76% of acromegaly patients moving in the predicted direction (P=0.0003) versus no significant shift in aging controls. The model achieved an AUC of 0.858 separating advanced acromegaly from controls on held-out photographs, and prediagnosis untreated baselines already showed modest separation from controls (AUC 0.65), raising the possibility of earlier recognition from ordinary photographs. This approach could eventually complement clinical screening by flagging subtle acromegaloid facial evolution before overt diagnosis, particularly in the primary care setting.
items.caveat: The sample with two usable timepoints was small (n=69), the longitudinal contrast strata trend was not statistically significant (P=0.15), and the study was cross-sectional/retrospective in design — prospective validation with standardized photography protocols is needed before any clinical deployment.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old patient presents with subtle coarsening of facial features over the past 4 years. IGF-1 is mildly elevated at 1.2× ULN; random GH is 1.1 ng/mL. Based on the machine-learning facial-change study published in EJE 2026, which statement best describes the potential utility of longitudinal photograph-based analysis in this scenario?
items.quiz_answer: The study demonstrated that acromegaly-associated facial change is measurable within individuals from ordinary photographs using a face-recognition model, and prediagnosis untreated faces already showed modest separation from controls (AUC 0.65). This suggests that longitudinal photograph-based scoring could serve as a non-invasive adjunct to biochemical testing to support earlier recognition, though it is not yet validated for clinical use and requires prospective confirmation.

items.title: Comparison of demographic, clinical and follow-up data of patients with micromegaly and acromegaly: a retrospective analysis from a single tertiary center.
items.summary: In this single-center retrospective review of 117 acromegaly patients, 14 (12%) met criteria for 'micromegaly' — defined by IGF-1 above ULN with GH <2 ng/mL and/or suppressed GH nadir <1 ng/mL plus classic clinical features. Despite lower GH levels and smaller, more often microadenoma-sized tumors, patients with micromegaly had comparable comorbidity profiles and clinical manifestations to classical acromegaly, underscoring that biochemically milder GH excess does not equate to clinically milder disease. Micromegaly patients had higher early postoperative biochemical control rates, but long-term remission rates were similar to classical acromegaly.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective design with a small micromegaly subgroup (n=14) limits generalizability. The biochemical definition of micromegaly lacks consensus standardization, and sensitivity analyses using alternative definitions were explored but a universally agreed threshold does not yet exist.
items.quiz_question: A 45-year-old woman has classic acromegaloid features — enlarged hands, prognathism, and hyperhidrosis — with IGF-1 at 1.4× ULN but a GH nadir of 0.8 ng/mL on OGTT and a baseline GH of 1.6 ng/mL. Imaging shows a 6 mm pituitary microadenoma. Based on the micromegaly study, what should guide your management approach?
items.quiz_answer: This presentation is consistent with 'micromegaly.' The study found that despite lower GH levels and smaller tumors, these patients have comorbidity and symptom burdens comparable to classical acromegaly. Apparently low GH does not indicate clinically mild disease, so full evaluation and treatment (including surgical consideration) remain warranted, similar to the approach for classical acromegaly.

items.title: Prevention and management of hormonal crisis in neuroendocrine tumors undergoing PRRT (peptide receptor radionuclide therapy): a systematic review.
items.summary: This systematic review of 28 studies examined hormonal crises during PRRT for functioning NETs, including carcinoid crisis (~1% incidence in available cohorts), insulinoma-related hypoglycemia, VIPoma crises, ectopic Cushing syndrome exacerbation, and catecholaminergic crisis in pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma. Hypoglycemic crises in insulinoma patients clustered around the first PRRT cycle, supporting inpatient glucose monitoring at that stage. Evidence across all syndromes was limited and heterogeneous, but consistently pointed toward pretreatment endocrine optimization, syndrome-specific prophylaxis, and multidisciplinary coordination as key safety pillars.
items.caveat: The evidence base is heavily case-report/retrospective-series dependent (18/28 studies); definitions of 'hormonal crisis' varied widely across studies, making incidence estimates unreliable. No firm protocol recommendations are possible from current data, and pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma crises during PRRT are represented by only small series.
items.quiz_question: You are preparing a patient with a functioning paraganglioma and somatostatin-receptor-positive metastatic disease for PRRT. Based on the 2026 systematic review on hormonal crises during PRRT, what pre-treatment considerations are most important for this patient's safety?
items.quiz_answer: The review identified catecholaminergic crisis as a recognized, albeit rare, complication of PRRT in pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma patients. Evidence — though limited to small series — consistently emphasized pretreatment endocrine optimization (adequate alpha-blockade, hemodynamic preparation), syndrome-specific prophylaxis, early recognition protocols, and multidisciplinary management. Structured risk assessment and periprocedural monitoring are considered essential, as harmonized management algorithms are not yet established.

items.title: Long-term post-trial extension of osilodrostat therapy in selected Canadian patients with Cushing disease from the LINC 3 and LINC 4 programs.
items.summary: This retrospective multicenter analysis followed 11 Canadian patients with Cushing disease who continued osilodrostat after completing the LINC 3 or LINC 4 trials, with 7 remaining on therapy long-term. Six of those 7 had controlled mean urinary free cortisol at last follow-up after a median exposure of 98 months (range 83–121 months), supporting durable biochemical control. Maintenance doses varied widely (median 6 mg/day, range 0.125–40 mg/day), and several patients required progressive dose down-titration over time, consistent with evolving sensitivity. Two patients experienced clinically significant pituitary tumor enlargement requiring discontinuation and surgery, underscoring that tumor surveillance remains mandatory during long-term steroidogenesis inhibitor therapy.
items.caveat: Highly selected cohort of only 11 patients continuing from industry-sponsored trials; 4 discontinued before the extension phase, introducing survivorship bias. Results are descriptive without inferential statistics, and this experience may not generalize to patients outside specialized centers or those who did not tolerate early therapy.
items.quiz_question: A 42-year-old woman with Cushing disease achieves biochemical control on osilodrostat 10 mg/day after failing transsphenoidal surgery. Five years into therapy her dose has been down-titrated to 2 mg/day to avoid hypocortisolism. What additional surveillance consideration does this long-term real-world cohort highlight beyond cortisol monitoring?
items.quiz_answer: Clinically significant pituitary tumor enlargement occurred in 2 of 11 patients in this cohort, leading to discontinuation and surgery. Ongoing pituitary MRI surveillance is essential for patients on long-term osilodrostat, as tumor growth can occur even during sustained biochemical control.

items.title: An Overview of Cushing's Syndrome Caused by Ectopic Adrenocorticotropin Secretion.
items.summary: This comprehensive review covers the full clinical and diagnostic landscape of ectopic Cushing's syndrome (ECS), which accounts for 10–20% of endogenous hypercortisolism. It delineates two phenotypic patterns: an aggressive presentation driven by rapidly growing tumors (e.g., small-cell lung carcinoma) featuring severe hypokalemia, myopathy, and hyperpigmentation without typical centripetal obesity, versus an indolent presentation from well-differentiated bronchial carcinoids that may closely mimic Cushing's disease. Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) is highlighted as the gold standard for distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH sources, though the review emphasizes that absence of a central-to-peripheral gradient supports—but does not itself localize—an ectopic source. Medical control of hypercortisolism with steroidogenesis inhibitors (metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat) or bilateral adrenalectomy is framed as a critical bridge while tumor localization is pursued, given that 10–20% of ectopic tumors remain occult on multimodality imaging.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without systematic methodology or pooled data; clinical heterogeneity across cited studies is substantial. Recommendations on steroidogenesis inhibitor choice are not derived from head-to-head trials.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of profound proximal weakness, blood pressure 180/110 mmHg, serum potassium 2.8 mEq/L, and markedly elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol. He lacks centripetal obesity. ACTH is 280 pg/mL. BIPSS shows a central-to-peripheral ACTH ratio of 1.4 (below the 2.0 cutoff). What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the priority next step?
items.quiz_answer: The clinical picture (acute severe hypercortisolism, hypokalemia, myopathy, absent centripetal obesity) combined with an elevated ACTH and a non-suppressed central-to-peripheral ACTH ratio on BIPSS is consistent with ectopic ACTH syndrome. The priority next step is multimodality tumor localization (high-resolution CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis followed by Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT) while initiating urgent medical adrenal blockade to control hypercortisolism and prevent life-threatening complications.

items.title: Mild Autonomous Cortisol Secretion Is Associated with Computed Tomography-Derived Hepatic Steatosis in Patients with Adrenal Incidentaloma.
items.summary: In this retrospective single-center study of 123 patients with adrenal incidentaloma (39 MACS, 84 NFAI), MACS was associated with subtle CT-derived hepatic fat accumulation compared to non-functioning adenomas, most clearly reflected in the liver-spleen attenuation difference (p = 0.048). Conventional CT-defined steatosis thresholds and non-invasive metabolic indices did not differ significantly between groups, suggesting that continuous CT attenuation parameters may be more sensitive for detecting subclinical hepatic lipid accumulation. Of the biochemical cortisol markers tested, only 24-hour urinary free cortisol correlated significantly with CT-derived hepatic attenuation parameters, including the liver-spleen attenuation difference after multivariable adjustment.
items.caveat: Retrospective design, modest sample size (especially the MACS group, n=39), and cross-sectional nature preclude causal inference. The borderline statistical thresholds (some p-values at 0.047–0.056) and lack of histologic validation (liver biopsy) limit confidence; prospective studies are needed before this influences routine practice.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old woman is referred for an incidentally found 2.3 cm lipid-rich left adrenal nodule. Her 1-mg overnight DST cortisol is 2.8 µg/dL (reference <1.8). She has no overt Cushingoid features but has BMI 29, mild hypertension, and borderline fasting glucose. Routine abdominal CT shows a liver attenuation of 48 HU and spleen attenuation of 62 HU. How does this imaging finding relate to her adrenal diagnosis?
items.quiz_answer: The liver-spleen attenuation difference is negative (liver 48 HU vs. spleen 62 HU), consistent with hepatic steatosis. According to this study, MACS—which her post-DST cortisol of 2.8 µg/dL suggests—is associated with subtle CT-derived hepatic fat accumulation, most sensitively detected by the liver-spleen attenuation difference rather than conventional steatosis thresholds. This reinforces the metabolic consequences of even mild autonomous cortisol excess and supports comprehensive cardiometabolic evaluation in MACS patients.

items.title: Cortisol in cardio-kidney-metabolic disease.
items.summary: This review synthesizes emerging evidence that hypercortisolism—spanning mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) to overt Cushing syndrome—is a substantially underrecognized driver of cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease. Prospective data cited include a 24% prevalence of hypercortisolism in difficult-to-control T2DM (CATALYST trial) and 27% in resistant hypertension (MOMENTUM trial), with MACS carrying a 2.5-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death. The authors propose the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test as the diagnostic test of choice and outline a therapeutic algorithm spanning steroidogenesis inhibitors, glucocorticoid receptor antagonists, and surgery for remediable disease.
items.caveat: Prevalence figures come from selected, phenotypically enriched cohorts rather than unselected CKM populations, so generalizability is uncertain. The review calls explicitly for standardized diagnostic thresholds and clinical trials before cortisol-targeted strategies can be routinely integrated into CKM care pathways.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old woman with obesity, longstanding resistant hypertension on four agents, and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has no classic Cushingoid features. Based on the evidence summarized in this review, what screening test should you consider, and what prevalence of hypercortisolism might you expect in this phenotype?
items.quiz_answer: The 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is the recommended first-line screen. In the MOMENTUM cohort of patients with resistant hypertension, the prevalence of hypercortisolism was approximately 27%, making biochemical screening reasonable in this high-pretest-probability CKM phenotype even without overt Cushingoid stigmata.

items.title: Optimizing inferior petrosal sinus sampling: results of a multicenter study.
items.summary: This multicenter RAPID registry analysis of 93 confirmed Cushing's disease patients evaluated whether IPSS protocols could be streamlined without sacrificing diagnostic sensitivity. At baseline, 77% of patients met a ≥2X central:peripheral ACTH ratio, and sensitivity rose to 91.4% by 15 minutes post-stimulation, with diagnostic yield plateauing at that point. The best post-stimulation ACTH responses occurred at 2–5 minutes, and the authors conclude that baseline plus a limited set of early post-stimulation samples (through 15 minutes) captures the vast majority of cases, potentially reducing laboratory and interpretive burden.
items.caveat: This is a retrospective, hypothesis-generating study limited to a surgically confirmed CD cohort, so the figures represent sensitivity rather than overall diagnostic accuracy (specificity cannot be assessed). Prospective validation with a standardized protocol is needed before protocol changes are adopted broadly. The 78% MRI-negative rate in this cohort may limit generalizability.
items.quiz_question: During an IPSS for a patient with biochemically confirmed ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome and a negative pituitary MRI, at what post-stimulation time point is the central:peripheral ACTH ratio most likely to peak, and at what time point does adding further samples yield negligible additional diagnostic information?
items.quiz_answer: According to this study, the highest fold-increase in C:P ACTH ratio occurred at 2–5 minutes post-stimulation. Diagnostic yield plateaued by 15 minutes, with negligible incremental gain from samples collected beyond that point, suggesting a streamlined protocol through 15 minutes post-stimulation is sufficient.

items.title: Evaluation of Diastolic Dysfunction in Pituitary Adenomas: A Comparative Single-Center Study Among Acromegaly, Prolactinoma, and Nonfunctioning Pituitary Adenomas.
items.summary: This cross-sectional study of 214 participants compared echocardiographic and cardiometabolic profiles across acromegaly, prolactinoma, NFPA, and healthy controls. Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (LVDD) was present in 46% of acromegaly patients versus only 5.8% of controls, and all three pituitary adenoma subtypes showed independently elevated LVDD odds compared to controls on multivariable analysis. Acromegaly was associated with the highest cardiometabolic burden (insulin resistance, glucose impairment) and the most pronounced diastolic abnormalities including elevated E/e' and reduced lateral e' velocity, predominantly grade I impaired relaxation.
items.caveat: Single-center, cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the very wide confidence intervals (e.g., OR 167.5 for acromegaly, 95% CI 10.3–2721.4) reflect small subgroup sizes—particularly the acromegaly group (n=26)—and should be interpreted with caution. Disease activity and treatment duration were not uniformly controlled across groups.
items.quiz_question: A 48-year-old man with biochemically active acromegaly reports no cardiac symptoms. Routine echocardiography is ordered. Based on this study's findings, what is the most likely diastolic dysfunction pattern you would expect, and what cardiometabolic parameter was most strongly elevated in the acromegaly group compared to controls?
items.quiz_answer: The most likely finding is grade I diastolic dysfunction (impaired relaxation pattern), which accounted for 84.8% of all LVDD cases in the cohort and was present in 46% of acromegaly patients. Fasting glucose, HbA1c, insulin, and HOMA-IR were all highest in the acromegaly group, reflecting the prominent insulin-resistant phenotype associated with GH/IGF-1 excess.
